content: # 4. External VOC anchor: complete selection logic
## 4.1 What the anchor does
The VOC anchor defines the external biological question and constrains candidate-program selection. It does not create a measured endpoint.
The formal anchor class is:
C4-C10 straight-chain saturated aliphatic aldehydes, meaning butanal, pentanal, hexanal, heptanal, octanal, nonanal, and decanal.

The term anchor class does not mean that all seven compounds are consistently increased in gastric cancer, that they form a validated diagnostic panel, that they share one exclusive source, or that this study measures any of them.
## 4.2 Selection criteria applied before effects
A VOC class was suitable for this project only if it jointly met the following criteria:
1. repeated appearance in human gastric-cancer-related breath literature;
2. at least some direct gastric-tissue or biologically proximal evidence;
3. a coherent, bounded host biochemical question that can be represented in public human transcriptomic and proteomic data;
4. separable generation-related and handling-related components;
5. enough shared chemistry to support one class-level question without treating unrelated molecules as one pathway; and
6. a defensible claim ceiling in the absence of direct VOC measurement.

Aldehydes best satisfy this combined requirement. This is a choice of mechanistic tractability and evidence coherence, not a claim that aldehydes are the most accurate, most specific, most abundant, or only relevant gastric-cancer VOCs.
## 4.3 Why aldehydes were selected over other reported VOC classes

The reviewed gastric-cancer literature includes aldehydes, ketones, hydrocarbons, alcohols, short-chain fatty acids, esters, aromatics, sulfur compounds, heterocycles, and other molecules. Their presence alone is insufficient for a molecular-program study.
| VOC class | Gastric-cancer literature signal | Principal reason it is not the primary anchor | Status in this plan |

| Straight-chain aldehydes | Repeated in upper-gastrointestinal and gastric breath studies; selected members also altered in paired gastric-tissue headspace | None of the available studies proves tumor-to-breath transfer, and some directions are inconsistent | Selected external anchor with explicit limitations |

| Ketones | Acetone, butanone, cyclohexanone, 2-pentanone, 2-nonanone, and long odd-chain methyl ketones have been reported | The class mixes systemic ketogenesis, broad carbonyl chemistry, cell-line-specific methyl-ketone patterns, and contradictory directions. Breath acetone is strongly affected by fasting and energy balance. The odd-chain methyl-ketone route lacks adequate independent human gastric replication for this project | Not part of the prespecified main line |

| Alkanes, alkenes, and isoprene | Multiple gastric studies report isoprene, cyclohexane, undecane, decane, and longer hydrocarbons | Directions are frequently inconsistent; isoprene is strongly shaped by non-cancer host physiology; hydrocarbons are difficult to map to a bounded human-tissue generation-and-handling program; ambient and material sources are important | Literature context only |

| Alcohols | Methanol, propanol, diols, and branched alcohols appear in breath, tissue, and cell-line work | Alcohol concentrations can be exposure-, diet-, oral-microbiome-, sampling-route-, and reversible-dehydrogenase-dependent. Gastric tissue and cell-line directions are heterogeneous | Literature context only |

| Short-chain fatty acids | Propionic, butyric, valeric, and hexanoic acids recur in gastric or oesophagogastric breath studies | These molecules strongly implicate microbial fermentation, gastrointestinal luminal biology, diet, systemic transport, and acid-base partitioning. Public gastric-tissue RNA and protein cannot adjudicate their breath source without microbiome, luminal, blood, and targeted chemical measurements | Important alternative biology, not a formal host-tissue program |

| Aromatics, halogenated compounds, sulfur compounds, and heterocycles | Individual studies report toluene, xylenes, chlorobenzene, dimethyl sulfide, pyridine, and related compounds | Exogenous exposure, diet, microbiota, medication, platform annotation, and source ambiguity are substantial; the reported molecules do not form one coherent host molecular program | Not a formal program |

This comparison deliberately acknowledges that the non-selected classes may be biologically important. They are not declared false. They are excluded from the prespecified core because including them would convert one answerable study into several weakly connected projects.
## 4.4 Why C4-C10 straight-chain saturated aldehydes were selected within aldehydes
The C4-C10 window is selected for six convergent reasons.
### 4.4.1 Repeated gastric and upper-gastrointestinal breath reporting
The locally audited breath literature contains repeated reports of butanal, pentanal, hexanal, heptanal, octanal, nonanal, and decanal.
- Kumar et al. reported an oesophageal/gastric adenocarcinoma breath panel containing the full C4-C10 straight-chain series.
- Markar et al. externally evaluated an oesophagogastric model that retained butanal and decanal with three fatty acids.
- Huang et al. identified pentanal, hexanal, octanal, and decanal among eight GC-associated breath carbonyls.
- Chen et al. included heptanal in a six-VOC GC panel.
- Other gastric breath reports contain nonanal or related aldehydes, although not always in the same direction.

These studies differ in disease grouping, sampling, analytical platform, identification confidence, control population, and direction. They support the class as a question anchor, not a pooled diagnostic effect.
The compound-level retention map is deliberately qualitative because the studies are not exchangeable and no pooled VOC effect is planned:
| Anchor member | Principal human evidence retained | Important boundary |
| Butanal | Reported in the Kumar oesophageal/gastric series and retained in the multicenter Markar model | Evidence is largely from mixed oesophagogastric disease rather than GC-only tissue |
| Pentanal | Reported in the Kumar series and the Huang GC carbonyl study | No paired gastric-tissue support in the reviewed corpus |

| Hexanal | Reported in breath studies including Kumar and Huang; higher in paired cancer-tissue headspace in the Latvian cohort of Mochalski 2023 | The tissue result did not reproduce in the second geographic cohort |
| Heptanal | Reported in the Kumar series and entered the Chen 2024 GC panel | Chen 2024 contains a heptane/heptanal direction inconsistency, so no direction is frozen from that study |
| Octanal | Reported in the Kumar series and the Huang GC carbonyl study | No paired gastric-tissue support in the reviewed corpus |

| Nonanal | Reported in the upper-gastrointestinal breath literature; higher in paired cancer-tissue headspace in the Ukrainian cohort of Mochalski 2023 | Breath direction is not treated as uniform, and the tissue result was cohort-specific |
| Decanal | Reported in the Kumar series, retained in the Markar multicenter model, and reported in the Huang GC carbonyl study | Repetition does not establish gastric specificity or tumor origin |
### 4.4.2 Direct gastric-tissue proximity

Paired ex vivo gastric-tissue headspace work reported greater hexanal in cancer tissue in one geographic cohort and greater nonanal in another. The fact that these signals were cohort-specific, rather than reproduced in both cohorts, is retained as evidence of heterogeneity. Tissue headspace is biologically closer than breath but still does not prove that a breath aldehyde originated in the tumor.
### 4.4.3 Shared lipid-oxidation compatibility

Experimental oxidation of polyunsaturated fatty acids can generate volatile aliphatic aldehydes including pentanal, hexanal, heptanal, and nonanal. This supports a bounded biochemical link between peroxidizable lipid substrates, lipid hydroperoxides, fragmentation products, and volatile alkanals.

This link remains incomplete in this project. The G program covers substrate assembly and enzymatic lipid-oxidation support; it does not measure the nonenzymatic fragmentation step, lipid species, iron, antioxidant state, aldehyde yield, or gas release.
### 4.4.4 A measurable healthy-breath background exists

C3-C10 saturated aldehydes have been directly quantified in healthy breath. In one 26-person SIFT-MS study, propanal was the most abundant and C4-C10 aldehydes were present only at trace median concentrations. A later 692-participant study quantified the entire C4-C10 straight-chain series, with nonanal and hexanal among the more abundant members, and explicitly documented hygiene-product confounding.
This population evidence supports technical measurability and the coherence of the C4-C10 analytical class. It does not establish cancer specificity.
### 4.4.5 The chain-length boundary improves biological and analytical coherence

C1-C3 aldehydes are excluded from the anchor because formaldehyde, acetaldehyde, and propanal have highly abundant and heterogeneous endogenous, microbial, dietary, exposure, and alcohol-related sources. Propanal was the most abundant saturated aldehyde in healthy breath in the SIFT-MS study, making it less useful as the lower boundary of a trace alkanal question.

Aldehydes longer than C10 have lower volatility and substantially less consistent gastric breath evidence in the reviewed corpus. The upper bound is therefore pragmatic rather than a universal physicochemical cutoff.

Branched, unsaturated, hydroxy-, aromatic, and multifunctional aldehydes are excluded because their reaction chemistry, enzyme preferences, and biological roles differ materially from the saturated straight-chain series. They remain relevant contextual carbonyls but cannot be silently pooled with the anchor.
### 4.4.6 The class supports a generation-versus-handling framework
The anchor can be investigated through two distinguishable host molecular configurations:
- availability and oxidation of peroxidizable PUFA-phospholipid substrates; and
- oxidative handling of medium- and fatty-aldehydes.

This is more coherent than treating all VOC-associated genes as one aldehyde metabolism pathway. The two configurations must remain separate because abundance in either direction does not establish actual production, clearance, accumulation, or exhalation.
## 4.5 Evidence cautions that must remain visible
1. The strongest C4-C10 breath series evidence includes oesophagogastric cohorts and is not purely gastric-cancer-specific.
2. The 2024 Cancer Letters paper is important prior work and must be discussed explicitly. It linked a GC breath panel to aldehyde oxidation and pyruvate metabolism using single-cell analysis.

3. That paper contains a heptanal/heptane directional inconsistency between its replication text and later biological interpretation. This plan therefore uses it as evidence that an aldehyde entered a GC panel, not as a frozen direction-of-effect source.
4. The 2023 paired gastric-tissue study found cohort-specific hexanal and nonanal changes and broad cross-population heterogeneity.
5. Breath aldehydes may be affected by scented products, oral sampling, inspired air, smoking, collection materials, and analytical annotation.
6. Neither repeated reporting nor biochemical plausibility proves tumor origin.
## 4.6 Reusable rationale for later Introduction and Figure 1
The following logic may be reused, with journal-appropriate editing:

Gastric-cancer breath studies have reported chemically diverse VOCs, but many classes are difficult to connect to a bounded host-tissue mechanism because they are strongly influenced by diet, ambient exposure, systemic fuel metabolism, or oral and gut microbial activity. Straight-chain saturated aldehydes were selected because several C4-C10 members recur in gastric or oesophagogastric breath studies, hexanal and nonanal have been observed in paired gastric-tissue headspace, the class is quantitatively measurable in human breath, and PUFA oxidation plus aldehyde-dehydrogenase chemistry provides separable generation-related and handling-related hypotheses. The C4-C10 class is therefore an external biochemical anchor, not a measured outcome or a claimed gastric-cancer-specific signature.
A suitable Figure 1 selection funnel is:
Reported GC-related VOC landscape
→ class-level comparison
→ aldehydes selected for repeated human evidence plus host biochemical tractability
→ C4-C10 straight-chain saturated series selected for shared chemistry, breath measurability, and tissue proximity
→ two separate molecular configurations, G and H
→ paired bulk replication, donor-aware single-cell context, paired protein evidence, and limited same-patient RNA-protein bridge
→ claim ceiling: biochemical compatibility only.
